Walthrough - Semi-Supervised and Association Rules

Jeff

March 11, 2026

Semi-supervised - Weak/Granular labeling

Let’s start with a (hacky) use-case for semi-supervised learning, based on a real research question we have about mouse lung tissues.

Suppose your response-labelling process is at a different granular level than what your observations are.

Example: You are not allowed to ask a US citizen how they voted in the US election, but you do know their demographic information. In this case, you may have a sample of 800 people from California (went to Democrats), and 800 people from Texas (went to Republicans). It may be a reasonable assumption that your (representative) California sample has more democrats, and your (representative) Texas sample has more republicans. But it would not be reasonable to assume the state labels apply to the citizens, and fit in a fully supervised fashion.

We can simulate to show this of course. We will assume there are some consistent, measurable traits of democrats and republicans that are not region-specific.

set.seed(23511)
library(mvtnorm)
cali_r <- rmvnorm(300, mean=c(2,2))
cali_d <- rmvnorm(500, mean=c(0,0))
tex_r <- rmvnorm(620, mean=c(2,2))
tex_d <- rmvnorm(180, mean=c(0,0))
cali <- rbind(cali_r, cali_d)
tex <- rbind(tex_r, tex_d)
alldat <- rbind(cali, tex)
statelab <- rep(c(2,1), each=800)
unknowntrue <- rep(c(1,2,1,2), times=c(300,500,620,180))
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(alldat, col=statelab, main="Labels We Actually Have")
plot(alldat, col=unknowntrue, main="True, Unknown Labels")

You can see, visually, where this is going. If we take a supervised approach on this granular label, our parameter estimation will be way off. Which means, if we’d actually like to use those to help describe the traits of the political parties, the supervised approach will be quite useless. Of course, our predictions for the model will suffer as well!

#supervised discriminant analysis
library(teigen)
supmod <- teigen(alldat, Gs=2, known=statelab, scale=FALSE, models = "UUUU", verbose=FALSE)
## Warning in teigen(alldat, Gs = 2, known = statelab, scale = FALSE, models =
## "UUUU", : No NAs in 'known' nor training vector supplied, all values have known
## classification (parameter estimation only)
trainpred <- predict(supmod, newdata=alldat)
table(unknowntrue, trainpred$classification)
##            
## unknowntrue   1   2
##           1 853  67
##           2  55 625
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(alldat, col=trainpred$classification, main="Supervised Predictions")
points(supmod$parameters$mean, col="blue", cex=1, pch="M")
plot(alldat, col=unknowntrue, main="True, Unknown Labels")

As expected, the group means are computed as nearly on top of one another. Our classification performance overall is okay, but there are some weird results from the plot. Also, since our normal densities are so similar for each group, our uncertainty in classification will be pretty high across the board. We can see this by just looking at a histogram for the probabilities associated with the groups:

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(trainpred$fuzzy[,1])
hist(trainpred$fuzzy[,2])

Compare this to if we DID have the correct labelling…

#supervised discriminant analysis, correct labels
library(teigen)
supmod2 <- teigen(alldat, Gs=2, known=unknowntrue, scale=FALSE, models = "UUUU", verbose=FALSE)
## Warning in teigen(alldat, Gs = 2, known = unknowntrue, scale = FALSE, models =
## "UUUU", : No NAs in 'known' nor training vector supplied, all values have known
## classification (parameter estimation only)
trainpred2 <- predict(supmod2, newdata=alldat)
table(unknowntrue, trainpred2$classification)
##            
## unknowntrue   1   2
##           1 868  52
##           2  65 615
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(alldat, col=trainpred2$classification, main="Supervised (Correct Label)")
points(supmod2$parameters$mean, col="blue", cex=1, pch="M")
plot(alldat, col=trainpred$classification, main="Supervised (Granular Label)")
points(supmod$parameters$mean, col="blue", cex=1, pch="M")

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(trainpred2$fuzzy[,1])
hist(trainpred2$fuzzy[,2])

So now we’ve seen the granular case, and the (impossible by the setup of our problem) best case scenario. Can we approximate the best case scenario using semi-supervised instead?

The basic idea is that we can label some subset of the observations using the granular label, and let the mixture model sort out the rest. The less we label, the closer we get to unsupervised (which would actually work okay in this scenario probably).

For no particular reason, let’s randomly sample 10% as firm labels.

#semi-supervised
library(teigen)
set.seed(35131)
substatelab <- rep(NA, nrow(alldat))
sampind <- sample(1:nrow(alldat), .1*nrow(alldat))
substatelab[sampind] <- statelab[sampind]
semimod <- teigen(alldat, Gs=2, init="uniform", known=substatelab, scale=FALSE, models = "UUUU", verbose=FALSE)
trainpred3 <- predict(semimod, newdata=alldat)
table(unknowntrue, semimod$classification)
##            
## unknowntrue   1   2
##           1 809 111
##           2  62 618
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(alldat, col=trainpred3$classification, main="Supervised Predictions")
points(semimod$parameters$mean, col="blue", cex=1, pch="M")
plot(alldat, col=trainpred2$classification, main="Supervised (Correct Label)")
points(supmod2$parameters$mean, col="blue", cex=1, pch="M")

Similar to the fully supervised on granular labels, we’re taking some observations as ‘known’ to be in the wrong group. Our misclassification rate has gone up, but the mean estimates are heading in the right direction. If, however, we have a reasonable guess of a few observations that we’re confident in labeling (think back to the bias labeling example from lecture), we can fix this problem! In fact, we can fix it with a very minimal number of correct labels.

Let’s suppose we were confident of one extreme citizen in each direction. That is, if someone measures high on both variables they are almost certainly a republican and if someone measures low on both then they are almost certainly a democrat…

#semi-supervised
library(teigen)
substatelab2 <- rep(NA, nrow(alldat))
extremeDem <- which.min(rowSums(alldat))
extremeRep <- which.max(rowSums(alldat))
substatelab2[extremeDem] <- 2
substatelab2[extremeRep] <- 1
semimod2 <- teigen(alldat, Gs=2, init="uniform", known=substatelab2, scale=FALSE, models = "UUUU", verbose=FALSE)
trainpred4 <- predict(semimod2, newdata=alldat)
table(unknowntrue, semimod2$classification)
##            
## unknowntrue   1   2
##           1 869  51
##           2  66 614
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(alldat, col=trainpred4$classification, main="Semi-Supervised Predictions")
points(semimod2$parameters$mean, col="blue", cex=1, pch="M")
plot(alldat, col=trainpred2$classification, main="Supervised (Correct Label)")
points(supmod2$parameters$mean, col="blue", cex=1, pch="M")

In case you’re interested in how this conceptually works with our mouse lung research question…we can label regions of the lung fairly easily as containing (or not) fibrotic tissue. Our observations, though, are measurements on individual cells within these regions. Even in fibrotic areas, cells will be a mix of both fibrotic and normal. Luckily, we are fairly confident that the normal tissue areas will not contain fibrotic cells — which actually makes the problem easier than our voting example! The equivalent in that case: being able to assume the California label applies to all its citizens, and only needing to relax the Texas label in a semi-supervised fashion.

Association Rules

We saw association rules in the context of actual transactions, but they can also be viewed on categorical data by using what’s commonly called one-hot encoding. All it means is making an indicator variable for each level of the factor. The arules package can coerce factors into the desired form using the as() function. Let’s check out some survey data…

#install.packages("arules")
#install.packages("effects")
library(arules)
## Loading required package: Matrix
## 
## Attaching package: 'arules'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
## 
##     abbreviate, write
library(effects)
## Loading required package: carData
## lattice theme set by effectsTheme()
## See ?effectsTheme for details.
data(WVS)
head(WVS)
##       poverty religion degree country age gender
## 1  Too Little      yes     no     USA  44   male
## 2 About Right      yes     no     USA  40 female
## 3  Too Little      yes     no     USA  36 female
## 4    Too Much      yes    yes     USA  25 female
## 5  Too Little      yes    yes     USA  39   male
## 6 About Right      yes     no     USA  80 female

Note that there is one numeric variable in here. Let’s investigate how broadly it varies

summary(WVS$age)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   18.00   31.00   43.00   45.04   58.00   92.00

Let’s discretize that measure to make it categorical according to four equally spaced intervals.

WVS$age <- discretize(WVS$age, method="interval", breaks=4)
table(WVS$age)
## 
## [18,36.5) [36.5,55) [55,73.5) [73.5,92] 
##      1985      1825      1208       363

Now we can feed this into the apriori algorithm

Code for Lecture (Grocery Example)

library(arules)
data("Groceries")
itemFrequencyPlot(Groceries, topN=20, type="absolute")

arun <- apriori(Groceries, parameter=list(supp = 0.001, conf = 0.8))
## Apriori
##

##  confidence minval smax arem  aval originalSupport maxtime support minlen

##  maxlen target  ext
